01 / CAPTURE

Set up your review

For your report only. Open the page under review in its own browser window before sharing, and keep this analyzer window visible beside it. A hidden analyzer (for example, another tab in the same window) receives no frames.

Presentation and optional area calibration

Enter the dimensions of the entire shared surface at standard browser zoom, not video resolution or just the player. Area uses the 341 × 256 reference field. Dimensions are reviewer supplied, not automatically verified. Restart after resizing. Test the largest presentation and each layout that changes the content.

Measurement point in the shared image

50 / 50 is the center. Place the point over the animation you want to measure. Detection still checks every sampled pixel.

Screenshots can contain private page content. They stay in browser memory until you download them or start another capture.

Screening, with human review.

This tool flags candidates. It does not certify a pass or failure. Small or missed flashes, red transitions, and the WCAG flash-area threshold need further evaluation.

Use Chrome or Edge on desktop over HTTPS or localhost. Choose the target tab in the browser’s sharing picker.

WHAT DOES THIS MEASURE?

Brightness over time, at the same screen location.

1. Relative luminance · Y

A dimensionless value from 0 (black) to 1 (white), calculated from captured sRGB pixels. It is not screen brightness in nits and is not a contrast ratio.

Y = 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B

R, G and B are linearized channel values. For an 8-bit channel c, let s=c/255: linear=s/12.92 when s≤0.04045, otherwise ((s+0.055)/1.055)^2.4.

2. Changes and complete pairs

A general-flash candidate requires two opposing luminance changes, each at least 0.10, with a darker state below 0.80. A black → white → black sequence is one complete pair. The detector counts pairs within a rolling second at each sampled pixel.

The peak is the largest count at any one sampled pixel. Four or more flags review; the flash area may still be below the allowed threshold.

3. Color, timing and evidence

Red candidates use linear-R/(R+G+B) ≥ 0.8 and accumulated CIE 1976 u′v′ excursions > 0.2 between color extrema. This experimental trajectory model is incomplete, including curved color paths and black chromaticity. A negative result never clears red flashing.

The output separates the selected-point Y trace from the first detected pixel’s trace and pair states. It includes RGB, frame min/mean/max Y, sampling checks and static screenshots. All negative results remain inconclusive. Neither frame averages nor capture-wide ΔY establish a flash.

03 / INTERPRETATION

Evidence for a review.
Never an automatic “pass.”

WCAG allows no more than three general or red flashes in any one-second period, or flashes below its area threshold (SC 2.3.1, Level A). SC 2.3.2 (Level AAA) removes the threshold exception: this tool reports a separate strict screen with no area or brightness exemption. SC 2.3.3 (Level AAA) covers motion triggered by interaction and is reviewed manually with the motion checklist. A flash is a pair of opposing transitions; a single brightness change is not a complete flash.

This prototype tracks luminance excursions at reduced-resolution pixels and uses a separate red-transition heuristic. It flags pixels with more than three completed pairs in a rolling second. With reviewer-supplied CSS dimensions it also measures sampled pair-completion area in a moving reference field and a conservative rolling spatial envelope. This remains incomplete area screening, not a conformance verdict.

Test autoplay, video, animations, interaction states, and different viewport sizes. Preserve the test conditions. Review suspicious segments with an established flash-analysis tool before writing a conformance finding.

What can this screening miss?

Small regions, gradual red changes, fine patterns, moving flashes, differently phased regions, offscreen content, short events between captured frames, and protected video. Scrolling and camera motion can also produce false positives. Even a high observed frame rate does not rule out aliasing.
